prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, exhibit impressive zero-shot capabilities; however, this performance is largely contingent on the concepts having been seen during the massive pre-training phase ("In-Pre-training" or IP concepts). There is a critical deficiency in handling "Out-of-Pretraining" (OOP) generalization—concepts that are completely absent from the pre-training dataset. While empirical evidence suggests that pre-trained image encoders can successfully cluster these unseen concepts visually, the zero-shot transfer fails significantly. This failure stems from a misalignment in the text encoder: the model does not know how to map valid visual clusters to their corresponding linguistic names when those names were never learned. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this phenomenon because they typically contain substantial overlaps with pre-training vocabularies.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the bottleneck for OOP generalization is not the visual representation, but the specific token embeddings of the unseen class names within the text encoder. Standard adaptation methods like prompt-tuning (optimizing the context around the class name) or adapters (adding layers to the visual backbone) are insufficient because they do not address the fundamental lack of initialization for the specific OOP concept tokens.

We propose "Name-Tuning" as a superior alternative. By specifically optimizing the embedding vectors of the new concept names while freezing the rest of the pre-trained model, we can achieve alignment. Furthermore, we hypothesize that we can achieve this even without labeled image-text pairs (zero-shot) by leveraging the structural consistency of visual clusters and matching them to candidate text embeddings via graph optimization.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to investigate a holistic framework for aligning OOP concepts, subdivided into a new evaluation benchmark and two learning algorithms.

**1. Benchmark Construction (LAION-Beyond)**
To rigorously isolate OOP performance, we will construct a benchmark that strictly segregates concepts into those present in standard large-scale pre-training datasets (IP) and those completely absent (OOP). This will ensure that our evaluation measures true generalization rather than memory retrieval.

**2. Few-Shot Name Learning (FSNL)**
For scenarios where a small number of labeled examples are available, we will implement a "Name-Tuning" strategy.
*   **Targeted Optimization:** Instead of tuning the prompt context or the visual backbone, we will only update the token embeddings of the specific OOP words.
*   **Context Shuffling Augmentation:** To prevent overfitting to the limited few-shot contexts, we will employ a data augmentation strategy that shuffles context templates across semantically similar concept pairs (e.g., swapping the sentence structure of two different animal descriptions). This forces the model to learn the semantic meaning of the name rather than the sentence syntax.

**3. Zero-Shot Name Learning (ZSNL)**
For scenarios with no image-text pairs (only a list of potential OOP names and a set of unlabeled images), we propose a two-step alignment process:
*   **Guided Clustering (Novel Class Discovery):** We will use the pre-trained image encoder to cluster the unlabeled OOP images. To ensure these clusters represent meaningful categories, we will guide the clustering process using supervision signals from known IP classes, effectively transferring knowledge about what constitutes a valid "object category."
*   **Bipartite Graph Matching:** We will compute the centroids of these visual clusters and the text embeddings of the candidate OOP names. We will then model the alignment problem as a bipartite graph matching task. By solving for the optimal assignment between visual centers and text embeddings, we will generate pseudo-labels for the clusters. These pseudo-labels will then drive the Name-Tuning process described in the FSNL module.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **True Generalization Benchmark:** A validated protocol for distinguishing between retrieval-based performance (IP) and genuine learning capability (OOP) in VLMs.
2.  **Theoretical Insight:** A demonstration that fine-tuning specific concept embeddings ("Name-Tuning") is more effective for unseen concepts than broad prompt adaptation.
3.  **Algorithmic Novelty:** A unified framework that enables VLMs to align completely new concepts in both data-scarce (few-shot) and label-free (zero-shot) environments, leveraging structural knowledge transfer from known to unknown classes.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **LAION-Beyond:** A constructed benchmark derived from LAION-400M, LAION-2B, and LAION-5B to isolate Out-of-Pretraining (OOP) concepts.
    *   **Composition:**
        *   **OOP Concepts:** 674 concepts absent from the pre-training vocabulary (106,052 images in the 400M split).
        *   **IP (In-Pretraining) Concepts:** 324 concepts present in the pre-training vocabulary (51,330 images in the 400M split).
    *   **Domains:** 9 domains arranged hierarchically: Plants_Fungi, Insects_Spiders, Animals, Pokemon, FolkArt, Landmark, Attire, Food, and Architecture.
    *   **Splits:** OOP images were divided into training, validation, and test sets. IP concepts were used solely for evaluation comparisons or novel class discovery guidance, not for supervised training of OOP names.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Clustering Accuracy:** Normalized clustering accuracy to measure feature discriminability.
    *   **Classification Accuracy (ACC):** Top-1 accuracy for open-vocabulary prediction.
    *   **Harmonic Mean (H-mean):** The harmonic mean of accuracy on IP classes and accuracy on OOP classes to measure trade-offs.
    *   **Class-Balanced Accuracy ($ACC_{cls-bal}$):** Used to debias performance regarding the different numbers of IP and OOP classes.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Zero-Shot Baselines:** OpenCLIP (variants), TransCLIP.
    *   **Few-Shot/Tuning Baselines:** CoOp, CoCoOp, CLIP-Adapter (Clip-Ada), TaskRes, Linear Probe, Learning-to-Name (L2Name/NTL).
    *   **Note:** Baselines were reproduced using OpenCLIP backbones to ensure fair comparison within the LAION-Beyond setup.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone:** OpenCLIP (variants trained on LAION-400M, 2B, and 5B).
    *   **Few-Shot Settings:** $N$-shot learning with $N \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16\}$.
    *   **Randomization:** Experiments repeated with 3 random seeds.
    *   **Optimization (FSNL):** "Name-tuning" methodology used InfoNCE loss to optimize token embeddings for OOP concepts while keeping image and text encoders frozen. Contexts were shuffled across similar concept pairs for augmentation.
    *   **Optimization (ZSNL):** Bipartite graph matching was used to align image cluster centers (initialized via Novel Class Discovery) with OOP name embeddings.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Clustering Margins (t-SNE):** We observed that image features extracted from OOP concepts exhibited significant clustering margins/gaps across categories, despite these concepts never being seen during pre-training. Furthermore, OOP concept clusters did not overlap with IP concept clusters, indicating inherent visual discriminability in the pre-trained encoder.
*   **Zero-Shot Generalization Failure:** While visual features were discriminative, zero-shot transfer failed significantly for OOP concepts compared to IP concepts. This gap persisted even when accounting for class imbalance.
*   **Neural Scaling Law Limitation:** We observed that increasing the pre-training scale (from LAION-400M to LAION-5B) improved IP performance but did not resolve the image-text misalignment for OOP concepts. In some cases (LAION-Beyond 2B), the gap between IP and OOP performance widened when class-balanced accuracy was considered.
*   **Linear Probe vs. Adapters:** In few-shot settings, a basic Linear Probe (using only image features) often rivaled or outperformed prompt-tuning and adapter-based approaches (CoOp, CoCoOp, TaskRes) on OOP domains. This suggested that existing VLM adaptation methods failed to effectively align the textual modality with the visual features of unseen concepts.
*   **Few-Shot Trajectory:** The FSNL method demonstrated consistent improvement over baselines across 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 shots. It showed a steeper learning curve, approaching the performance upper bound more rapidly than adapters or prompt tuning.
*   **Context Augmentation Ablation:** In ablation studies, we found that augmenting training with contexts from similar concepts (Categorical Ancient branching) provided performance gains over pure embedding tuning, though pure embedding tuning alone still outperformed the OpenCLIP baseline.
*   **IP Knowledge in Zero-Shot:** We found that TransCLIP, which attempts to transfer IP knowledge, provided trivial benefits for OOP zero-shot learning. In contrast, ZSNL, which utilizes IP knowledge to guide clustering (Novel Class Discovery) followed by bipartite matching, achieved significant improvements.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP and its variants, rely heavily on the alignment of visual and textual information established during massive pre-training. While these models exhibit strong zero-shot capabilities, existing evaluations primarily focus on "In-Pretraining" (IP) concepts—visual concepts that, while perhaps unseen in the specific downstream task, were present within the massive web-scale datasets used for pre-training.

There is a critical gap in understanding and addressing **Out-of-Pretraining (OOP)** generalization. When a VLM encounters a concept effectively absent from its pre-training corpus (e.g., a rare biological species or a newly coined artifact name), the text encoder lacks the specific token embedding initialization required to generate a meaningful classification weight. Existing adaptation methods, such as prompt-tuning or adapters, presuppose that the underlying token embeddings contain valid semantic signals. However, for OOP concepts, these embeddings are often arbitrarily initialized or effectively random, leading to a breakdown in cross-modal alignment. We currently lack both a rigorous benchmark to isolate OOP concepts and a data-efficient methodology to align these concepts without extensive model re-training.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the failure of VLMs on OOP concepts is not due to a lack of visual discriminability—the image encoder likely clusters OOP visual features distinctly—but rather due to **image-text misalignment** caused by uninitialized name embeddings in the text encoder.

We propose that:
1.  **Name-Tuning:** Directly optimizing the specific token embeddings of OOP names (while freezing the rest of the model) is theoretically superior to prompt-tuning or adapters for this class of problem.
2.  **Context Augmentation:** For Few-Shot scenarios, shuffling contexts across semantically related concept pairs will force the model to learn the specific name embedding rather than overfitting to background context.
3.  **Graph Matching for Zero-Shot:** For Zero-Shot scenarios (where we have OOP images but no labels), we can align unsupervised visual clusters with OOP text embeddings via bipartite graph matching to generate pseudo-labels for self-supervised name-tuning.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Benchmark Construction: LAION-Beyond
To rigorously separate IP and OOP performance, we will construct a new benchmark, **LAION-Beyond**. We will define IP concepts as those present in the vocabulary of standard pre-training datasets (LAION-400M, LAION-2B), and OOP concepts as those strictly absent from these lexical scopes.
We will curate images across 9 hierarchical domains (e.g., Plants/Fungi, Insects/Spiders, Folk Art). For each domain, we will ensure a distribution of both IP and OOP classes to facilitate direct comparative analysis of generalization mechanisms.

### 2. Theoretical Formulation of Name-Tuning
We utilize an OpenCLIP architecture with an image encoder $f$ and a text encoder $g$. The standard probability of a class $y$ given image $\pmb{I}$ is:

$$ P_{V}^{(f,g)}(\pmb{y} | \pmb{I}) = \frac{\exp \big( \frac{\sin(f(\pmb{I}), g(\pmb{T}(\pmb{y})))}{\gamma} \big)}{\sum_{\pmb{y}_i \in V} \exp \big( \frac{\sin(f(\pmb{I}), g(\pmb{T}(\pmb{y}_i)))}{\gamma} \big)} $$

Where $\pmb{T}(\pmb{y})$ is a prompt template containing the class name (e.g., "a photo of a $\{\pmb{y}\}$").

For OOP concepts $Y_{OOP}$, the embedding $e(\pmb{y})$ is uninitialized. We propose **Name-Tuning**, where we freeze $f$ and $g$ and exclusively optimize the token embeddings for the set $Y_{OOP}$. Given a set of OOP image-text pairs $\{\langle \hat{I}(y), \hat{T}(e(y)) \rangle\}$, the optimization objective is:

$$ \operatorname*{min}_{e(y) \in e(Y_{OOP})} \hat{\mathcal{R}}_{Y_{OOP}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}} \Big( \langle \hat{I}(y), \hat{T}(e(y)) \rangle \Big) $$

Here, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ represents the contrastive loss. This formulation aligns the specific OOP token embeddings into the shared visual-semantic space established by the frozen encoders.

### 3. Algorithm 1: Few-Shot Name Learning (FSNL)
In the few-shot setting (limited labeled OOP images), we will employ two strategies to prevent overfitting:

**A. Initialization via Language Models:**
Instead of random initialization, we will initialize OOP word embeddings using tokenized inputs passed through a standard BERT-like language model to capture prior linguistic semantics.

**B. Context Shuffling Augmentation:**
We will augment the training data by shuffling prompt contexts. Let $P_{CS}$ denote a distribution of prompts generated by swapping contexts between similar concept pairs (e.g., swapping "A woman in a..." with "People dressed in..." for the same class label). We effectively force the optimization to focus on the class token $e(\pmb{y})$ rather than the context. The augmented objective is:

$$ \operatorname*{min}_{e(\pmb{y}), \forall \pmb{y} \sim \pmb{Y}_{\mathrm{OOP}}} \sum_{\hat{\pmb{T}}_j \sim P_{\mathrm{CS}}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}} \bigg( \sum_{\hat{\pmb{T}}_j \sim P_{\mathrm{CS}}} \big< \hat{\pmb{I}}(\pmb{y}), \hat{\pmb{T}}_j(e(\pmb{y})) \big> \bigg) $$

### 4. Algorithm 2: Zero-Shot Name Learning (ZSNL)
In the zero-shot setting, we possess a set of unlabeled images $\{\hat{I}(y)\}$ belonging to OOP classes and a list of candidate OOP class names, but no mapping between them. We propose a three-step pipeline:

**Step 1: Cluster Initialization via Novel Class Discovery (NCD)**
We will leverage knowledge from IP classes to guide the clustering of OOP images. We will freeze the image encoder backbone $f(\cdot)$ and train a classification head using NCD techniques to cluster the unlabeled OOP images into distinct visual groups.

**Step 2: Image-Text Bipartite Graph Matching**
We will compute the normalized average feature vector for each resulting image cluster to serve as the cluster center. Simultaneously, we will generate prompt embeddings for all candidate OOP names using the text encoder $g$.
We will construct a bipartite graph where edge weights represent the cosine similarity between image cluster centers and OOP prompt embeddings. We will then apply the **Hungarian Algorithm** to solve for the optimal global assignment, generating pseudo-labels for the clusters.

**Step 3: Self-Supervised Name-Tuning**
Using the high-confidence pseudo-labeled samples from the bipartite matching, we will apply the Name-Tuning objective (Eq. 2) to optimize the name embeddings, thereby achieving zero-shot alignment.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Metric Isolation:** The establishment of the **LAION-Beyond** benchmark will provide the community with the first standard for distinguishing between In-Pretraining recall and true Out-of-Pretraining generalization.
2.  **Theoretical Insight:** We expect to formally define the generalization bound for OOP concepts and demonstrate via Proposition that prompt-tuning is insufficient for uninitialized concepts compared to name-tuning.
3.  **Algorithmic Solution:** The **FSNL** and **ZSNL** algorithms will provide a data-efficient framework for adapting large-scale VLMs to open-world concepts without the prohibitive cost of full model fine-tuning or the need for extensive labeled data.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
